opener.label: Before any chemistry

steps.pre: How many stacks can you make from 6 eggs?
steps.say: A kitchen puzzle, no chemistry yet. The recipe is fixed: every stack needs 2 eggs.

steps.pre: For those 3 stacks, how many cups of flour?
steps.say: You just scaled a recipe by its ratio. The bigger recipe also needs 3 cups of flour per stack.
steps.hint: 3 cups for each of the 3 stacks.

steps.say: A balanced equation is exactly this recipe. In \(2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O\) the big numbers (2, 1, 2) are the ratio, just like eggs to stacks. Chemists count in moles instead of eggs and scale the same way. The one extra move is swapping between grams and moles using moles = mass ÷ Mr.

steps: Balance by changing coefficients only, never the formulae.
Convert the known mass to moles: moles = mass ÷ Mr.
Scale the moles using the ratio from the coefficients.
Convert back to mass: mass = moles × Mr.
method_card.title: Balancing Equations and Reacting Masses
method_card.content:
Reacting mass questions follow one chain: mass → moles → ratio → mass.

First balance the equation, then read the mole ratio from the big numbers in front of each formula. Convert the mass you are given into moles with moles = mass ÷ Mr, scale by the ratio, and convert back with mass = moles × Mr.

Show every step: method marks are available even when the final number is wrong. Watch for changing a subscript instead of a coefficient, skipping the ratio, or working from the wrong substance.

steps: The same three moves apply, but the equations are less familiar and the formula masses larger, so work slowly.
Build each Mr from its atoms before you start, and take the ratio straight from the coefficients.
Convert back to mass and reverse-check the answer.
gold.title: Gold: the full chain, trickier equations

example.question: In C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O, find the mass of CO2 from 22 g of propane. (Mr: C3H8 = 44, CO2 = 44)

steps: Turn the known mass into moles with moles = mass ÷ Mr.
The coefficients give the ratio. When it is 1:1, the moles of the product equal the moles of the reactant.
Turn moles back into mass with mass = moles × Mr, then reverse-check.
bronze.title: Bronze: one equation, a 1:1 ratio

example.question: In 2Ca + O2 → 2CaO, find the mass of CaO from 40 g of Ca. (Mr: Ca = 40, CaO = 56)

steps: Find the moles of the known substance as before.
Read the ratio from the coefficients. If it is 2:1, halve the moles; if 1:2, double them; for 3:2, multiply by 2 then divide by 3.
Convert the scaled moles back to mass, then check.
silver.title: Silver: scale by the mole ratio

example.question: In 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3, find the mass of Fe2O3 from 112 g of Fe. (Mr: Fe = 56, Fe2O3 = 160)

exam_context.frequency: High. Reacting mass questions appear in most chemistry papers.

gold.hint: One mole of Al gives one mole of AlCl3 (2:2); build the AlCl3 Mr from all three chlorines.
gold.display: In 2Al + 3Cl2 → 2AlCl3, calculate the mass of AlCl3 produced from 27 g of Al. (Mr: Al = 27, AlCl3 = 133.5)

guided_steps.say: Reacting mass is one chain: mass to moles, then the ratio, then back to mass. Start with the known substance, Al: moles = mass ÷ Mr.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the given mass by the relative formula mass.

guided_steps.say: The balanced equation has 2 Al to 2 AlCl3, a 1:1 ratio, so the moles of AlCl3 equal the moles of Al.

guided_steps.hint: Apply the ratio from the balanced equation to the moles you found.
Multiply the moles of AlCl3 by its relative formula mass.

guided_steps.done: Back to 1 mol AlCl3, matching the ratio, so 133.5 g is right.
guided_steps.hint: Mass divided by Mr should return the moles of AlCl3.

misconceptions.message: Mr AlCl3 = 27 + (3 × 35.5) = 27 + 106.5 = 133.5. Do not forget all three chlorines.
1 is the moles of AlCl3. Convert to mass: 1 × 133.5 = 133.5 g.

gold.hint: Convert 4 g of H2 to moles, the 2H2 : 2H2O ratio is 1:1, then convert back to mass.
gold.display: In 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, calculate the mass of water produced from 4 g of H2. (Mr: H2 = 2, H2O = 18)

guided_steps.say: Reacting mass is one chain: mass to moles, then the ratio, then back to mass. Start with the known substance, H2: moles = mass ÷ Mr.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the given mass by the relative formula mass.

guided_steps.say: The balanced equation has 2 H2 to 2 H2O, which is a 1:1 ratio, so the moles of H2O equal the moles of H2.

guided_steps.hint: Apply the ratio from the balanced equation to the moles you found.
Multiply the moles of H2O by its relative formula mass.

guided_steps.done: Back to 2 mol H2O, matching the ratio, so 36 g is right.
guided_steps.hint: Mass divided by Mr should return the moles of H2O.

misconceptions.message: The ratio 2H2 : 2H2O is 1:1, so 2 mol H2 gives 2 mol H2O, mass = 2 × 18 = 36 g.
2 is the moles of water. Convert to mass: 2 × 18 = 36 g.

gold.hint: Convert 32 g of CH4 to moles, the CH4 : CO2 ratio is 1:1, then convert back using the CO2 Mr.
gold.display: Methane combustion: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. Calculate the mass of CO2 produced from 32 g of CH4. (Mr: CH4 = 16, CO2 = 44)

guided_steps.say: Reacting mass is one chain: mass to moles, then the ratio, then back to mass. Start with the known substance, CH4: moles = mass ÷ Mr.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the given mass by the relative formula mass.

guided_steps.say: The balanced equation has 1 CH4 to 1 CO2, a 1:1 ratio, so the moles of CO2 equal the moles of CH4.

guided_steps.hint: Apply the ratio from the balanced equation to the moles you found.
Multiply the moles of CO2 by its relative formula mass.

guided_steps.done: Back to 2 mol CO2, matching the ratio, so 88 g is right.
guided_steps.hint: Mass divided by Mr should return the moles of CO2.

misconceptions.message: Convert using the Mr of CO2 (44), not CH4 (16). Moles CH4 = 2, ratio 1:1, mass = 2 × 44 = 88 g.
2 is the moles of CO2. Convert to mass: 2 × 44 = 88 g.

bronze.hint: Find moles of CuCO3, keep the same moles of CuO (1:1), then convert back to mass.
bronze.display: In CuCO3 → CuO + CO2, what mass of CuO is produced from 62 g of CuCO3? (Mr: CuCO3 = 124, CuO = 80)

guided_steps.say: Reacting mass is one chain: mass to moles, then the ratio, then back to mass. Start with the known substance, CuCO3: moles = mass ÷ Mr.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the given mass by the relative formula mass.

guided_steps.say: The balanced equation CuCO3 → CuO + CO2 has a 1:1 ratio of CuCO3 to CuO, so the moles of CuO equal the moles of CuCO3.

guided_steps.hint: Apply the ratio from the balanced equation to the moles you found.
Multiply the moles of CuO by its relative formula mass.

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.5 mol CuO, matching the ratio, so 40 g is right.
guided_steps.hint: Mass divided by Mr should return the moles of CuO.

bronze.equation_hint: Moles = mass ÷ Mr, then use 1:1 ratio, then mass = moles × Mr

misconceptions.message: Moles = mass ÷ Mr, not Mr ÷ mass. 62 ÷ 124 = 0.5 mol, then 0.5 × 80 = 40 g.
0.5 is the moles of CuO. Finish by converting to mass: 0.5 × 80 = 40 g.

bronze.hint: Convert 48 g of Mg to moles, the ratio is 1:1, then convert back to mass.
bronze.display: In 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO, what mass of MgO is produced from 48 g of Mg? (Mr: Mg = 24, MgO = 40)

guided_steps.say: Reacting mass is one chain: mass to moles, then the ratio, then back to mass. Start with the known substance, Mg: moles = mass ÷ Mr.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the given mass by the relative formula mass.

guided_steps.say: The balanced equation 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO has 2 Mg to 2 MgO, which is a 1:1 ratio, so the moles of MgO equal the moles of Mg.

guided_steps.hint: Apply the ratio from the balanced equation to the moles you found.
Multiply the moles of MgO by its relative formula mass.

guided_steps.done: Back to 2 mol MgO, matching the ratio, so 80 g is right.
guided_steps.hint: Mass divided by Mr should return the moles of MgO.

misconceptions.message: Moles = mass ÷ Mr: 48 ÷ 24 = 2 mol, then 2 × 40 = 80 g. Dividing Mr by mass gives the wrong start.
2 is the moles of MgO. Convert to mass: 2 × 40 = 80 g.

bronze.hint: One mole of CaCO3 gives one mole of CO2; convert moles back to mass with the CO2 Mr.
bronze.display: In CaCO3 → CaO + CO2, what mass of CO2 is produced from 100 g of CaCO3? (Mr: CaCO3 = 100, CO2 = 44)

guided_steps.say: Reacting mass is one chain: mass to moles, then the ratio, then back to mass. Start with the known substance, CaCO3: moles = mass ÷ Mr.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the given mass by the relative formula mass.

guided_steps.say: The balanced equation CaCO3 → CaO + CO2 has a 1:1 ratio of CaCO3 to CO2, so the moles of CO2 equal the moles of CaCO3.

guided_steps.hint: Apply the ratio from the balanced equation to the moles you found.
Multiply the moles of CO2 by its relative formula mass.

guided_steps.done: Back to 1 mol CO2, matching the ratio, so 44 g is right.
guided_steps.hint: Mass divided by Mr should return the moles of CO2.

misconceptions.message: The CO2 does not keep the mass of the CaCO3. Moles CaCO3 = 1, ratio 1:1, moles CO2 = 1, mass = 1 × 44 = 44 g.
1 is the moles of CO2. Convert to mass: 1 × 44 = 44 g.

bronze.hint: Divide the mass by the Ar of iron.
bronze.display: How many moles are in 56 g of iron? (Ar of Fe = 56)

guided_steps.say: Just one move here: moles = mass ÷ Ar. For iron the Ar is 56.

guided_steps.hint: 56 divided by 56.

guided_steps.say: Always sanity-check a moles answer by reversing it: mass = moles × Ar should give back the mass in the question.

guided_steps.hint: Multiply your moles by the Ar.

guided_steps.done: Back to 1 mol, and 1 × 56 = 56 g matches the question. Correct: 1 mol.
guided_steps.hint: Mass divided by Ar returns the moles.

misconceptions.message: Moles = mass ÷ Ar = 56 ÷ 56 = 1 mol. Multiplying (56 × 56) is the slip.

bronze.hint: The ratio Na : H2 is 2:1, so divide the sodium moles by 2.
bronze.display: In 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2, how many moles of H2 are produced from 4 mol of Na?

guided_steps.say: The ratio comes straight from the coefficients of 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2: two Na to one H2.

guided_steps.hint: Read the big number written before Na.

guided_steps.say: So the ratio Na : H2 is 2:1. Divide the sodium moles by 2.

guided_steps.hint: Halve the 4 mol of sodium.

guided_steps.done: That returns the 4 mol of sodium, so 2 mol H2 is right.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply the H2 moles back up by 2.

misconceptions.message: The ratio Na : H2 is 2:1, not 1:1. So 4 mol Na gives 4 ÷ 2 = 2 mol H2.
Divide by 2, do not multiply: 4 ÷ 2 = 2 mol H2.

silver.hint: The ratio Fe : Fe2O3 is 2:1, so halve the iron moles before converting to mass.
silver.display: In 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3, calculate the mass of Fe2O3 produced from 56 g of iron. (Mr: Fe = 56, Fe2O3 = 160)

guided_steps.say: Reacting mass is one chain: mass to moles, then the ratio, then back to mass. Start with the known substance, Fe: moles = mass ÷ Mr.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the given mass by the relative formula mass.

guided_steps.say: The balanced equation has 4 Fe to 2 Fe2O3, which simplifies to 2:1. So divide the iron moles by 2.

guided_steps.hint: Apply the ratio from the balanced equation to the moles you found.
Multiply the moles of Fe2O3 by its relative formula mass.

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.5 mol Fe2O3, matching the ratio, so 80 g is right.
guided_steps.hint: Mass divided by Mr should return the moles of Fe2O3.

misconceptions.message: The ratio Fe : Fe2O3 is 4:2 = 2:1, not 1:1. Moles Fe2O3 = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5, mass = 0.5 × 160 = 80 g.
Divide the iron moles by 2, do not multiply: 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5 mol Fe2O3, mass = 0.5 × 160 = 80 g.

silver.hint: The ratio N2 : NH3 is 1:2, so double the nitrogen moles before converting to mass.
silver.display: In N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, calculate the mass of ammonia produced from 28 g of N2. (Mr: N2 = 28, NH3 = 17)

guided_steps.say: Reacting mass is one chain: mass to moles, then the ratio, then back to mass. Start with the known substance, N2: moles = mass ÷ Mr.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the given mass by the relative formula mass.

guided_steps.say: The balanced equation has 1 N2 to 2 NH3, a 1:2 ratio. So multiply the nitrogen moles by 2.

guided_steps.hint: Apply the ratio from the balanced equation to the moles you found.
Multiply the moles of NH3 by its relative formula mass.

guided_steps.done: Back to 2 mol NH3, matching the ratio, so 34 g is right.
guided_steps.hint: Mass divided by Mr should return the moles of NH3.

misconceptions.message: The ratio N2 : NH3 is 1:2, not 1:1. Moles NH3 = 1 × 2 = 2, mass = 2 × 17 = 34 g.
2 is the moles of NH3. Convert to mass: 2 × 17 = 34 g.

silver.hint: The ratio H2 : NH3 is 3:2, so multiply the hydrogen moles by 2 and divide by 3.
silver.display: In N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, calculate the mass of ammonia produced from 12 g of H2. (Mr: H2 = 2, NH3 = 17)

guided_steps.say: Reacting mass is one chain: mass to moles, then the ratio, then back to mass. Start with the known substance, H2: moles = mass ÷ Mr.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the given mass by the relative formula mass.

guided_steps.say: The balanced equation has 3 H2 to 2 NH3, a 3:2 ratio. So multiply the hydrogen moles by 2, then divide by 3.

guided_steps.hint: Apply the ratio from the balanced equation to the moles you found.
Multiply the moles of NH3 by its relative formula mass.

guided_steps.done: Back to 4 mol NH3, matching the ratio, so 68 g is right.
guided_steps.hint: Mass divided by Mr should return the moles of NH3.

misconceptions.message: The ratio H2 : NH3 is 3:2, not 1:1. Moles NH3 = 6 × 2 ÷ 3 = 4, mass = 4 × 17 = 68 g.
4 is the moles of NH3. Convert to mass: 4 × 17 = 68 g.

silver.hint: Convert 13 g of Zn to moles, the ratio is 1:1, then convert back with the ZnO Mr.
silver.display: Zinc reacts with oxygen: 2Zn + O2 → 2ZnO. Calculate the mass of ZnO produced from 13 g of Zn. (Mr: Zn = 65, ZnO = 81)

guided_steps.say: Reacting mass is one chain: mass to moles, then the ratio, then back to mass. Start with the known substance, Zn: moles = mass ÷ Mr.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the given mass by the relative formula mass.

guided_steps.say: The balanced equation has 2 Zn to 2 ZnO, a 1:1 ratio, so the moles of ZnO equal the moles of Zn.

guided_steps.hint: Apply the ratio from the balanced equation to the moles you found.
Multiply the moles of ZnO by its relative formula mass.

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.2 mol ZnO, matching the ratio, so 16.2 g is right.
guided_steps.hint: Mass divided by Mr should return the moles of ZnO.

misconceptions.message: Moles = mass ÷ Mr: 13 ÷ 65 = 0.2 mol, then 0.2 × 81 = 16.2 g. Dividing Mr by mass gives the wrong start.
0.2 is the moles of ZnO. Convert to mass: 0.2 × 81 = 16.2 g.

problem_bank.gold_description: The full mass, moles, ratio, mass chain on less familiar equations with larger formula masses, so track every coefficient and Mr.
problem_bank.bronze_description: One equation given, a 1:1 mole ratio, masses already in grams: convert to moles, keep the moles, convert back.
problem_bank.silver_description: The mole ratio is not always 1:1, so scale the moles up or down using the balanced coefficients before converting back to mass.
